items.question: Why does figurative usage fail to establish real agency in the self?
premises: Figurative usage does not attain the real nature of a thing.
A merely figurative designation may be devoid of real substance.
A designation lacking real substance cannot establish actual agency.
items.inference: Therefore, attributing agency to the self by figurative usage does not prove that the self is truly an agent.
items.plain_english: Figurative usage does not reach the real nature of a thing; such a designation may be empty of reality, so it cannot establish real agency.

items.question: What follows if agency is attributed to the self only by figurative designation?
premises: A merely figurative designation does not make something what it is called.
Even if a person were figuratively called fire, he would not remove cold caused by snow, hail, showers, and wind.
Real causal power requires more than a figurative name.
items.inference: Therefore, figuratively calling the self an agent does not give it real causal efficacy.
items.plain_english: Even if someone were called fire only figuratively, he would not remove the cold caused by snow, hail, showers, and wind.

rows.grounds: subject of second clause; sandhi ca+anyaḥ

items.question: If the self is not truly an agent, who could bear agency even figuratively?
premises: Prakṛti is not declared to be the seer of the seeing self.
No other candidate exists to take over agency from the self.
Figurative agency still requires some locus to which it can be attributed.
items.inference: Therefore, there is no suitable bearer for even a figurative attribution of agency.
items.plain_english: Prakṛti is not called the seer of the self, and there is no other candidate left; so there is no one to whom agency could even be figuratively assigned.

items.question: What practical purpose does a merely figurative attribution of agency serve?
premises: A figurative usage of agency has no clear explanatory purpose.
A mere designation, even if unreal, can still be changed or replaced.
What can be altered without loss of reality does not establish real agency.
items.inference: Therefore, the figurative attribution of agency is explanatorily dispensable.
items.plain_english: What purpose is served by talk of agency if it is only figurative? Such a designation need not be real and can simply be changed.

items.question: What challenge is posed to those who accept the self as an agent?
premises: Some doctrinal thinkers accept the self as an agent.
Accepting agency requires explaining what kind of agency is meant.
The author poses a prior question to test that explanation.
items.inference: Therefore, those who affirm the self's agency must first answer what kind of agency they attribute to it.
items.plain_english: Even those who, following their doctrine, accept the self as an agent must first answer this question that we put to them.

items.question: Can ordinary action-based agency apply to an all-pervading self without vibration?
premises: Ordinary agency is established through connection with action.
Such ordinary agency involves vibration or movement.
The all-pervading self is described as devoid of vibration.
items.inference: Therefore, ordinary action-based agency does not fit an all-pervading, vibrationless self.
items.plain_english: Can the kind of agency known from ordinary action, which involves vibration, really belong to an all-pervading self that has no vibration?

rows.grounds: third member of triad; sandhi yatnaḥ
appositive to the three; compound = guṇa+traya

items.question: How do opponents define agency in the self without invoking vibration?
premises: Opponents propose knowledge, desire to act, and effort as a triad.
This triad is said to belong to the self.
They identify the possession of this triad as agency.
items.inference: The opponent's position is that agency consists in the self's possession of knowledge, desire to act, and effort.
items.plain_english: The objection is: knowledge, desire to act, and effort form a triad belonging to the self, and that is what is called agency.

items.question: How does the author evaluate the opponent's definition of agency?
premises: The proposed definition is presented as misleading.
It could deceive only those with childish understanding.
Even children are not entirely devoid of awareness.
items.inference: Therefore, the opponent's definition of agency is too weak to withstand scrutiny.
items.plain_english: This kind of reasoning might deceive the childish, but even children are not without awareness.

items.question: Why does the triad of knowledge, desire, and effort fail to define agency?
premises: Knowledge by itself is not agency because it is present everywhere.
Desire and effort are also generally present in many cases.
What is widely present without producing action cannot be the defining mark of agency.
items.inference: Therefore, the mere presence of knowledge, desire, and effort does not constitute agency.
items.plain_english: Knowledge is not agency, since it is present everywhere; and desire and effort too are generally found in everyone, so their mere presence does not amount to agency.

items.question: Can knowledge, desire, and effort by themselves produce an action?
premises: A potter may know, desire, and make effort to have a house.
Despite possessing these three, he may still fail to make a house for himself.
Agency requires more than the mere presence of the triad.
items.inference: Therefore, knowledge, desire, and effort are insufficient to constitute real agency.
items.plain_english: A potter distressed by not having a house may know, want, and try, yet still be unable to make a house for himself.

items.question: Does lack of know-how explain why the potter cannot build the house?
premises: An opponent may claim the potter does not know how to do it.
From that lack of know-how, desire and effort would also be absent.
If the relevant know-how is absent, the action cannot occur.
items.inference: The objection tries to preserve the triad theory by saying the potter lacks the specific knowledge of doing.
items.plain_english: The objection says: he does not know how to do it, so he does not want to do it and does not try; then how could he make the house?

rows.grounds: genitive of the verbal root sense; sandhi karoteḥ

items.question: What does the qualifier 'to do' add to knowledge, desire, and effort?
premises: The opponent qualifies knowledge, desire, and effort with the phrase 'to do'.
This qualifier must have a determinate meaning.
One possible meaning is that it implies vibration or dynamic activity.
items.inference: The debate turns on whether 'to do' adds a real dynamic factor beyond the triad.
items.plain_english: If knowledge, desire, and effort are qualified by 'to do', what does that qualifier mean? Does it mean having vibration?

items.question: If 'to do' means vibration, where is that vibration located in an all-pervading self?
premises: If agency means vibration, the self would know and desire to vibrate.
Any such vibration would have to be located in the self.
An all-pervading self, by its nature, does not admit such produced vibration.
items.inference: Therefore, interpreting 'to do' as vibration does not rescue agency for an all-pervading self.
items.plain_english: If 'to do' meant vibration, the statement would be that he knows and wants to vibrate; but such vibration cannot belong to an all-pervading self.

rows.grounds: subject of second clause; compound = jñāna+icchā+yatna+vattva

items.question: Can knowledge without vibration explain agency even in the highest subject?
premises: Knowledge entirely without vibration is not admissible, even for Śiva.
The opponent treats the triad as an instrument of agency.
An instrumental account still does not show the self as the true agent.
items.inference: Therefore, redefining agency through a vibrationless triad fails to establish real agency.
uncertainties: The reading śarvasyāpi follows the transmitted text; some editions may normalize the name differently.
items.plain_english: A knowledge without vibration would not be possible even for Śiva, and merely having knowledge, desire, and effort has been described only as an instrument, not as true agency.

items.question: What does the phrase 'of the self, to do' amount to when analyzed?
premises: The phrase 'to do' must be analyzed in terms of the self's acts.
Analysis yields knowing, desiring, and striving.
These can be further specified as knowing to know, striving to strive, and desiring to desire.
items.inference: The analysis reduces 'to do' to internal cognitive-volitional acts rather than external agency.
items.plain_english: When we analyze the meaning of 'the self is to do', it comes down to knowing, desiring, and striving — even striving to know, to desire, and to strive.

rows.grounds: subject of result clause; compound = cikīrṣitṛ+tva
verb of result clause; sandhi syāt

items.question: Does analyzing 'to do' into separate mental acts yield real agency?
premises: Taken individually, the analysis yields knowing to do and desiring to do.
Being a desirer to act is not the same as being an agent.
A verbal analysis of 'to do' does not by itself produce agency.
items.inference: Therefore, the proposed analysis yields only desire or cognition, not genuine agency.
items.plain_english: Taken one by one, this analysis amounts to knowing to do and wanting to do; that makes one a desirer to act, but not truly an agent.

rows.grounds: instrumental in second question; compound = vāc+kāya+karman

items.question: If agency is only mental, how can bodily and verbal actions belong to the agent?
premises: If agency is defined only by mental factors, speech and bodily actions become equivalent to mental ones in the wrong way.
Alternatively, it becomes unclear how speech and bodily actions could belong to the same agent.
A theory of agency must account for mental, verbal, and bodily action together.
items.inference: Therefore, defining agency by the mental triad alone fails to explain agency in speech and bodily action.
items.plain_english: If that were so, speech and bodily actions would be wrongly equated with mental ones; or else how could agency in speech and body belong to the same agent?

items.question: How can even mental actions be attributed to the self on the triad theory?
premises: The opponent appeals to the presence of the triad of qualities.
Actions arise from mind, speech, and body.
The mere presence of the triad does not explain how these actions belong to the self.
items.inference: Therefore, the triad theory does not adequately explain the self's ownership of any class of actions.
items.plain_english: Even if that triad is present, explain how mental actions — and likewise actions arising from mind, speech, and body — can truly belong to him.

rows.grounds: ablative/genitive sense in compound context; sandhi saṃciteḥ
predicate with quotation; compound = karman+bhāgin + iti

items.question: Can accumulated karma make the self a real agent rather than a figurative one?
premises: An opponent may say the self is the sharer of accumulated actions.
Calling the self a sharer of action can still be only figurative.
A figurative attribution does not establish real agency.
items.inference: Therefore, appeal to accumulated karma does not overcome the charge of figurative agency.
items.plain_english: If one says the self is the sharer of accumulated actions, that too would be only figurative usage — and that has already been shown to be inadequate.

items.question: Does mere proximity to qualities of the self make it the locus of agency?
premises: Qualities such as motion, greatness, and others may be present in relation to the self.
Mere presence or proximity of qualities does not by itself constitute agency.
A locus of agency must be more than a passive substrate near qualities.
items.inference: Therefore, the self does not become an agent merely because certain qualities are present with it.
uncertainties: The compound ātmagamahattvādi is compressed; the exact list of qualities intended is not fully explicit in this verse.
items.plain_english: Just because qualities such as motion, greatness, and others are present in relation to the self, does that make the self a locus of agency?

items.question: What unwanted consequence follows if proximity to qualities makes one an agent?
premises: If proximity to qualities were enough, agency could arise even in liberation.
The same rule would apply when qualities of another self are nearby.
A theory that yields agency in liberation or by another's qualities is unacceptable.
items.inference: Therefore, proximity to qualities cannot be the basis of agency.
items.plain_english: That cannot be accepted, because then agency would arise even in liberation, and the same rule would apply when the qualities of another self are nearby.

items.question: What further doctrinal faults follow from mislocating agency in selves?
premises: If agency is wrongly assigned among selves, karmic accounting breaks down.
This would produce loss of what has been done and arrival of what has not been done.
The discussion then turns to whether the Lord is needed as cause in intelligent arrangements.
items.inference: Therefore, misplacing agency leads to karmic disorder and raises the question of the Lord's causal role.
items.plain_english: Then, among selves, there would arise the faults of losing what has been done and gaining what has not been done; and what about the Lord's role in effects everywhere that require intelligence?

items.question: If material and accessory causes are complete, what room remains for an intelligent agent?
premises: An opponent may assign efficient causality to the Lord in effects with complex arrangement.
Such effects may already be fully supplied by inherent and other causal factors.
If all causal factors are complete, an extra efficient agent seems unnecessary.
items.inference: The opponent challenges the need for the Lord's efficient causality when material conditions are sufficient.
items.plain_english: If efficient causality is assigned to the Lord in a complexly arranged effect, what happens when that effect is already fully supplied by its own inherent and other causal factors?

items.question: Can the Lord's causality be modeled on the partial causality of agents like a potter?
premises: Ordinary agents like potters contribute only a partial causal factor.
The all-doer cannot be limited to contributing a mere part.
There is no trace of such partial contribution in the all-doer.
items.inference: Therefore, the Lord's causality cannot be understood on the model of ordinary finite agents.
items.plain_english: What partial contribution, like that of a potter, could be assigned as the Lord's causality? In the all-doer there is not even the slightest trace of such a partial role.
